clue.text: Game that calls for thirst quenchers

definitions.meaning: a board game played with round pieces on a chequered board
long swallows of a drink, deep gulps that quench a thirst

explanation.surface: A game so taxing that the players keep calling for drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: The board game played on a chequered board shares its name with deep gulps of drink, one of the two senses of the word.

parts.note: a North American spring wildflower is named after the baggy trousers of a man from the Netherlands

explanation.surface: A man whose trousers are covered in flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: Dutchman's breeches is a wild flower whose blooms look like baggy pantaloons.
explanation.definitionFit: The wildflower Dicentra cucullaria is called Dutchman's breeches, so this man's breeches are a flower.

parts.note: bootless means fruitless; on the first of April people are sent on pointless errands as a prank

explanation.surface: A barefoot messenger boy who works annually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bootless' reads as shoeless, but it means fruitless: on 1 April the victim is sent on a fool's errand.
explanation.definitionFit: The victim of a prank on 1 April is sent on a pointless errand, a futile messenger once a year.

definitions.meaning: the German heavy bomber of the First World War, named after its maker's town
the Almanach de ..., the directory of European royalty and nobility

explanation.surface: An almanac that takes to the air.
explanation.definitionFit: A German town gave its name both to a WWI bomber aircraft and to a famous genealogical yearbook of royalty.

clue.text: For writing old prescriptions? Just what the doctor ordered

definitions.text: For writing old prescriptions? Just what the doctor ordered

parts.words: For writing old prescriptions? Just what the doctor ordered
parts.note: ancient writing was done on flat slabs of clay, wax or stone, and a doctor orders pills

explanation.surface: A doctor's prescriptions written in an old style.
explanation.walkthrough: The word covers both the wax or clay slabs used for writing in antiquity and the pills a doctor prescribes.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient writers used flat slabs to write on, and a doctor's prescription is often for pills of the same name.

parts.note: the Authorised Version says 'if thy right eye ... cause thee to stumble', using a verb meaning to trip someone up in their faith

explanation.surface: A definition of what it means to cause someone to stumble, in scriptural terms.
explanation.walkthrough: In the King James Bible the verb for causing someone to sin or stumble is the one we now use for giving insult: 'if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out'.
explanation.definitionFit: The scriptural verb meant to cause someone to stumble or sin, which is now the everyday word for causing hurt feelings.

clue.text: Speed the ships to the headland

parts.note: a fleet is a body of ships
a ness is a promontory, as in Scottish place names

explanation.surface: Sending ships quickly to a cape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speed' looks like a verb urging the ships on; it is the noun defining the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being fleet means being swift, so the quality is swiftness.

clue.text: Does she shed one tear, love ?

indicators.note: to shed is to cast off and scatter, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A question whether a woman weeps for her beloved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shed' scatters TEAR with O (love, zero in tennis); she is the Muse of love poetry, so 'love' hints at her too.
explanation.definitionFit: The Muse of lyric and love poetry is a woman of Greek myth, so the pronoun stands for her.

parts.note: a gap-fill from Wordsworth's sonnet London, 1802, where Milton's heart took on humble tasks and obligations

explanation.surface: A quotation from Wordsworth with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'London, 1802' Wordsworth says of Milton: 'and yet thy heart / The lowliest duties on herself did lay'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word names the humble tasks and obligations Milton's heart took upon itself.

definitions.meaning: a lack or shortcoming, a fault
to desert one's country or party for the opposition

explanation.surface: A wish to swap allegiance.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun it is a shortfall or flaw; as a verb it is to desert to the opposing side.

clue.text: For record time in the loco yards ?

definitions.text: For record time in the loco yards

parts.words: For record time in the loco yards
parts.note: two pictures in one phrase: the revolving platform a gramophone record spins on, and the rotating track used to turn engines round in railway yards

explanation.surface: A locomotive yard setting a speed record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For record time' reads as speed, but it is the spinning deck of a record player; railway yards had a rotating section of track to turn locomotives.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotating platform serves both a gramophone, spinning the disc, and a railway yard, swinging an engine round to face the other way.

indicators.note: upsetting the letters of the word knocks them into a new order

explanation.surface: A politician knocks over the water jug.
explanation.walkthrough: William Ewart was a nineteenth-century Liberal statesman who introduced the Public Libraries Act; 'upsets' rearranges WATER.
explanation.definitionFit: William Ewart was a Victorian Liberal member of parliament, a political figure remembered for public libraries reform.

parts.note: the sister in L. P. Hartley's novels about a brother and sister, who would naturally ask after her brother

explanation.surface: A woman looking for someone called Eustace.
explanation.walkthrough: L. P. Hartley's trilogy is titled 'Eustace and Hilda'; the clue imagines the sister asking where her brother has got to.
explanation.definitionFit: In L. P. Hartley's novels the sister of Eustace bears this name, so she is the one asking after him.

clue.text: Conductor when only V.I.P.s went awheel

parts.note: the elect are a chosen few, the most important people
rode means travelled on wheels, as on a bicycle or carriage

explanation.surface: A time when only important people could travel on wheels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' suggests a bus or orchestra, but it is an electrical conductor; 'the elect' are a chosen elite.
explanation.definitionFit: An electrode is a conductor through which electric current enters or leaves a cell or circuit.

clue.text: Jack goes to the dogs (how vulgar !) and is rich

parts.note: a jack, or jack tar, is a sailor, abbreviated AB for able seaman

indicators.note: a dropped initial aitch marks speech as common, so the opening H of the dogs' word goes

parts.note: hounds are hunting dogs

explanation.surface: A sailor goes to ruin, and yet he is wealthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes to the dogs' looks like the idiom for ruin; here AB is placed before 'OUNDS, the dogs with the H dropped as in Cockney speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that abounds is plentiful, so 'is rich' in the sense of being well supplied.

clue.text: Chela's relatives get a wee drink

parts.note: a chela is a crab's or lobster's claw, a nipper
kin are one's relations

explanation.surface: A guru's disciple's family have a small drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chela' looks like a disciple of a guru, but it is also a crustacean's claw.
explanation.definitionFit: A nipperkin is an old measure of liquor, a small cupful of half a pint or less.

parts.note: the Seven Against ..., in Aeschylus's play, were seven champions marching on one Greek city

explanation.surface: A goal for a team of seven.
explanation.walkthrough: Aeschylus's tragedy 'Seven Against Thebes' names the city the seven champions attacked. The printed grid shows R for B, a letter no crossing checks.
explanation.definitionFit: The seven champions of Greek legend marched against a single city, and capturing it was their aim.

parts.note: an area reserved for the privileged, the in-crowd, such as the members' area at a racecourse

explanation.surface: Something reserved for fashionable people.
explanation.walkthrough: The fenced area at a racecourse is for those let in, and also for the 'in' crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A fenced-off area keeps some people inside it, as at a racecourse where members are admitted.

parts.note: a draughtsman draws up a plan
the person drawing is a gent, a man

explanation.surface: A loud man who draws.
explanation.walkthrough: The draughtsman is a 'plan gent', a man of plans; 'draughtsman' also hints at the game at 1 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Plangent means loud and resonant, as of a mournful ringing sound.

clue.text: Rabbit works in a knowing way

indicators.note: the works are placed inside the word for knowing

parts.note: fly is slang for knowing or sharp-witted
ops is short for opera, the plural of opus, a work

explanation.surface: A rabbit that goes about its business shrewdly.
explanation.walkthrough: Flopsy is one of Beatrix Potter's Flopsy Bunnies; OPS goes inside FLY.
explanation.definitionFit: One of Beatrix Potter's bunnies, the sister of Mopsy and Cotton-tail, is a fictional rabbit of this name.

parts.note: Thackeray wrote letters in the voice of a footman named after his plush livery of one colour

explanation.surface: Letters that are luxuriously soft.
explanation.walkthrough: Thackeray's 'The Yellowplush Correspondence' is narrated by a footman; the answer is the colour before 'plush'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thackeray's footman narrator Charles James Yellowplush is named for the gold-coloured plush of his livery.

parts.note: a gap-fill: Milton's Il Penseroso describes the nightingale's song with a missing adjective meaning tuneful

explanation.surface: A quotation from Milton with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'Il Penseroso' Milton calls the nightingale's song 'Most musical, most melancholy'; the solver fills the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing adjective in Milton's line describes birdsong as tuneful and melodious.

parts.note: in the Dublin song, Molly Malone wheels her barrow crying her shellfish 'alive, alive-o'

explanation.surface: The goods a street seller pushes in her cart.
explanation.walkthrough: Molly Malone sold 'cockles and mussels, alive, alive-o' from her wheelbarrow; 'Lively' is the 'alive-o'.
explanation.definitionFit: Molly Malone's song names the shellfish she sold live from her barrow.

parts.note: 7 down is one of the nine Muses, so the way she entertained is in the manner of a Muse

explanation.surface: A question about how the entry at 7 entertained.
explanation.walkthrough: The Muse at 7 entertained 'a-mused', and to be entertained is also to be amused.
explanation.definitionFit: Being entertained leaves one diverted, and the Muse at 7 would do it 'a-Mused'.

clue.text: Old Roman on the Elsinore platform

definitions.text: Old Roman on the Elsinore platform

parts.words: Old Roman on the Elsinore platform
parts.note: in the opening scene of Hamlet officers keep watch on the battlements at Elsinore, and one bears the name of a Roman general

explanation.surface: An ancient Roman standing on the castle ramparts of Elsinore.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet opens on the platform before the castle at Elsinore, where the officer sees the ghost; his name was also borne by a Roman consul.
explanation.definitionFit: The officer who first sees the ghost in Hamlet shares a name with the Roman general who took Syracuse.

clue.text: Space, we hear, for poetic tears

indicators.note: the clue says the word for space sounds like the answer when spoken

parts.note: room is space, as in room to move

explanation.surface: Somewhere for poets to weep.
explanation.walkthrough: In older usage, 'room' and 'rheum' could be pronounced alike; Shakespeare uses rheum for tears.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheum is a watery discharge, used in poetry and Shakespeare for tears.

parts.note: a pupil of Rugby School is a Rugbeian, the most famous being Tom of Tom's Schooldays, and a deep reverie is a study of that colour

explanation.surface: The question of what a pupil at Rugby School studies.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Brown's Schooldays is set at Rugby School, so a Rugbeian's 'study' is a brown study, a fit of deep musing.
explanation.definitionFit: A 'brown study' is a deep reverie, and Tom Brown is the best-known pupil of Rugby School.

clue.text: Artist with Scottish footballer coming up in India

indicators.note: in a down entry coming up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician
a Hib is a player for Hibernian, the Edinburgh club

explanation.surface: A painter travels in India with a Scottish football player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' reverses RA plus HIB together to give BIHAR. Hibernian is an Edinburgh football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Bihar is a state of eastern India, so it lies within the country.

parts.note: produce suggests vegetables like the leek, while the glossy things are those with a smooth shining surface

explanation.surface: A request to make one of a set of glosses.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means smooth and glossy; 'Produce' also hints at the vegetable LEEK within it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleek describes a smooth, shining surface, one of the qualities of a gloss.

clue.text: Hospitality that must cut down stately homes profit

parts.words: that must cut down stately homes profit
parts.note: a stately home thrown open to paying visitors loses its owners' privacy, so freely open hospitality eats into that

explanation.surface: Generous hospitality that eats into the earnings of stately homes.
explanation.walkthrough: Stately homes that open to the public charge admission; keeping 'open house', welcoming all for free, would cut that income.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping open house means offering a ready welcome to all visitors, a form of generous hospitality.

clue.text: Fiscal request without so much as a please

definitions.text: Fiscal request without so much as a please

parts.words: Fiscal request without so much as a please
parts.note: a tax notice from the authorities insisting on payment, not politely asking

explanation.surface: The taxman asking for money without any politeness.
explanation.walkthrough: A tax demand is the fiscal request; a demand, unlike a request, is made without 'please'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tax demand is the formal notice requiring payment, a request made as an order.

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase stand in for, or are exchanged for, a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A soup tureen meant for those who are hungry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is tureen for' makes the letters of IS TUREEN become the answer when rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Esurient is a learned word meaning greedy or famished, from the Latin for being hungry.
